Overview
Students in the PhD in Physics gain a solid background in fundamental physics, and
demonstrate their ability to carry out research and overcome new challenges in a specific
area of interest. Our students often go on to traditional research positions at universities
and national labs as well as to industrial labs. Other careers pursued by PhD graduates
might include medical physics, analysis in technological and financial settings, and
data science.
Beyond the standard PhD in Physics, our program offers two concentrations for students
with more specific interests: a PhD Degree in Physics with Concentration in Astronomy
and a PhD Degree in Physics with Concentration in Physical Biology.
The learning goals for the PhD degree are as follows:
Should have mastered core physics and should be familiar with areas of physics outside
their research specialty.
Should be able to think independently and have acquired critical reasoning skills.
Should be an expert in their research specialty and have demonstrated the ability
to conduct original research.
Should be able to communicate research results to an audience of physicists.
Full requirements for the standard program and concentrations, along with the funding
package and tuition waiver typical of a PhD, are given in the sections below.
Steps to the PhD
Becoming a PhD in Physics happens in two phases: first advancing to candidacy by completing
coursework and passing your exams, then conducting original doctoral research and
defending it. The tables below lay out both phases in order; every milestone in them
is covered in full detail in its own section further down this page.
Phase I: Advancing to Candidacy
Timing
Milestone
Start in Year 1 before the summer; complete before Year 3
Find an advisor – essential; needed for the Oral Exam and to advance to candidacy. See Finding an Advisor and the Oral Exam.
One year into research; complete before Year 4
Oral Exam – present a research topic to demonstrate readiness for PhD-level research. See Finding an Advisor and the Oral Exam.
Years 1-2
Core Courses: 501, 505, 511, 512, 540. Courses may be waived based on the Comprehensive Exam, or
on prior graduate coursework – see Courses & Waivers.
Years 1-2
Non-core Courses: one of the Lab Courses 515 or 517, or a waiver; 3 Advanced Courses with breadth;
two semesters of teaching PHY 600; and PHY 598 and PHY 599 – see Courses & Waivers and Teaching and Graduate Seminars.
Start in Year 1; complete before Year 3
Comprehensive Exam – offered twice a year; students pass each core subject separately, one or two at
a time, over the first two years. See The Comprehensive Exam.
Advancing to candidacy means finding an advisor, completing the required coursework
or receiving the corresponding waiver, and passing both the Comprehensive Exam and
the Oral Exam – these don’t have to happen in a fixed order, and the Oral Exam is
often completed while coursework or the Comprehensive Exam are still in progress.
Each is covered in its own section below.
You must advance to candidacy at least one year before you defend your doctoral thesis.
Phase II: Doctoral Research
Timing
Milestone
After candidacy
Research – conduct original research; check in periodically with your thesis committee on
your progress.
After candidacy
Thesis – write according to the format of the graduate school; file forms, watch deadlines.
Final step
Defend Thesis – the thesis should be completed at least two weeks before the defense.
Once you’ve advanced to candidacy, the focus shifts to research: working with your
advisor, checking in periodically with your thesis committee, and ultimately writing
and defending your dissertation.
Two concentrations – an Astronomy Concentration and a Physical Biology Concentration – modify the course and exam requirements for students in the concentration; see
the bottom of this page for details.
Courses & Waivers: Core, Lab, Breadth
Only courses with a grade B or better are counted towards the PhD degree.
Core Courses
One of the requirements for advancement to candidacy is demonstration of command of
four core areas of physics: Classical Mechanics (PHY 501), Electricity and Magnetism
(PHY 505), Quantum Mechanics (PHY 511/512) and Statistical Mechanics and Thermodynamics
(PHY 540). Students who do not obtain waivers should begin taking the core courses
in their first semester. If a core course is not passed, it can either be retaken,
or the Comprehensive Exam can serve as a substitute – see Good Standing for the details.
Lab Requirement
PHY 515 or PHY 517 – these laboratory courses provide an introduction to the special
problems of experimental physics or observational astronomy, respectively. Students
perform a number of classical and instructive labs to learn why and how we acquire
the knowledge upon which physics is based.
Core Course and Lab Waivers
Waivers may be granted for required courses – core courses, breadth requirements,
teaching experience, PHY 515, etc. – on the basis of work done at other universities.
Requests must be made during the first semester of study at Stony Brook, directed
to the Graduate Program Director; a transcript alone is not sufficient, so the student
should also bring supporting documentation such as a detailed course syllabus, course
WEB pages, and homework assignments.
For a core course specifically, a waiver can be granted two ways. The first is by
taking advanced graduate courses covering equivalent material elsewhere, subject to
approval by an Advising Committee appointed by the Graduate Program Director. The
second is through the Comprehensive Exam. Passing the Comprehensive Exam at the Placement
level in a subject automatically exempts a student from the corresponding core course;
a strong but not quite Placement-level performance can still earn a waiver, at the
discretion of the Graduate Program Director, with input from the Advising Committee.
In the case of the Graduate Laboratory course (PHY 515 or PHY 517) all materials associated
with the course taken elsewhere should be presented: syllabus, the faculty supplied
instructions or “write-ups” of the experiments done by the student, the laboratory
logbook in which the student recorded the day-to-day results of each experiment, and
the final written report for each experiment, together with the grades for each of
those. Students seeking a waiver in PHY 515 or PHY 517 should submit all materials
to faculty teaching the course soon after arrival to Stony Brook. Instead of fully
waiving the course requirement, waivers are sometimes granted for individual experiments.
Breadth Requirement
All PhD students must take at least three advanced courses from the table below (or
courses approved by the Graduate Program Director), with at least one course from
an area of physics outside the student’s own field of research.
A few exceptions, all requiring the Graduate Program Director’s approval:
A course from the PHY 680 or PHY 690 series (i.e. Special Topics courses) may count
twice toward this requirement, provided the two offerings cover markedly different
topics.
PHY 503 may, in some circumstances, also count toward breadth.
A course from outside the Department may fulfill this requirement, provided it’s closely
related to physics research – see Taking Courses Outside the Department in Resources for the approval process.

Teaching and Graduate Seminars
Teaching
PHY 600 Teaching (two semesters) – because teaching and research are inextricably
intertwined in a scientist’s career, all PhD students are required to teach (be a
TA) for two semesters. Many do this for a second year. The first introduction to teaching
begins during the orientation week: entering students participate in a TA training,
required for all new TA’s. Usually graduate students will conduct laboratory sections
associated with undergraduate courses. Senior faculty members closely supervise this
effort. Students normally do their teaching concurrently with their own first year
courses, and earn 0-3 academic credits per semester in PHY 600.
Graduate Seminars
PHY 598 and PHY 599 are required of all PhD, MSI, and MA students. Almost everybody
should take them during their first two semesters at Stony Brook, as they provide
a good way to get acquainted with the department. The courses cover different areas
of physics and can be taken in any order.
In these seminars, students gain experience presenting research topics to an audience
of their peers. This requires different skills than the core courses: the level of
knowledge between speaker and listeners is nearly on a par, and the motivation for
the activity is different too. This prepares graduate students for presenting research
at seminars and scientific meetings, as well as for their own thesis defense.
PHY 664 (Astro Journal Club) or PHY 655 (Advanced Graduate Seminar) can be used as
a discretionary substitution for one of PHY 598 or PHY 599. This substitution requires
prior approval from both the Graduate Program Director and the course instructors.
The Comprehensive Exam
One of the requirements for a PhD in Physics is comprehension of core physics and
facility in problem solving at the graduate level. The Comprehensive Exam broadly
aligns with the content and technical level of the graduate core-course exams, but
is more comprehensive in scope.
Format and Level. The exam is offered over four days, during the week before the start of classes in
August and January, and covers four subjects: Classical Mechanics (CM), relativity
and Electricity&Magnetism (EM), Quantum Mechanics (QM), and Statistical Mechanics
and thermodynamics (SM). Each subject exam is four hours long and may be passed separately,
e.g. you may pass one subject each time the Comprehensive is offered. An effort will
be made to test each subject separately, but sometimes a strict separation isn’t possible.
Each subject may be passed at one of three levels. At the Placement level, all three
problems are considered and a high score is required – passing at the Placement level
automatically exempts the student from the corresponding core course. At the PhD and
Master levels, only the best two of the three problems are considered and each passing
level requires progressively lower scores. The faculty set the threshold these passing
levels after the subject exams are graded, weighing that year’s student performance
as a whole, historical norms, and absolute standards.
Timeline for Passing. As you complete the core courses, we recommend you take two subjects each semester
of your first and second year, so all four are done well within the deadline. If you
fail a single subject you simply retake that subject at the next sitting. All PhD
students are expected to pass the Comprehensive Exam – at least three subjects at
the PhD level and one at the Master level – before the start of their third year.
Students typically pass by the beginning of the fourth semester; those with more advanced
backgrounds often pass in the first year. We encourage all incoming students to take
an exam in a subject or two – you may pass, and there’s no disgrace or harm in an
unsuccessful attempt.
If You Don’t Pass on Time. If you haven’t fully passed by the beginning of your fifth semester, you should consult
the Graduate Program Director and set up an ad hoc committee to evaluate your progress
on the past exams, standing in required courses, and research potential. By working
with this committee, you should resolve the Comprehensive Exam requirements by the
end of the third academic year – see Good Standing below for the full process.
For the notes policy, grading process, and study resources, see The Comprehensive Exam in Resources.
Waivers. A transfer student who has already passed a written comprehensive exam as a matriculated
doctoral student in physics or astronomy at another university may request a waiver
of the Stony Brook exam – see The Comprehensive Exam in Resources for how to apply.
Finding an Advisor and the Oral Exam
Finding an Advisor and Starting Research. Our first advice is to start early: begin talking to potential advisors in your first
two semesters, perhaps by presenting a relevant topic in the Graduate Seminar. Try
to work with a research advisor over the summer after your first year, when coursework
isn’t competing for your time.
Students interested in formal theory typically arrive having completed the equivalent
of some of our core courses. They are encouraged to pursue course waivers (e.g., for
PHY 511) and take Quantum Field Theory during their first year to be ready to enter
research over the first summer and second year.
Both theoretical and experimental students should start working on a project and reading
broadly with supervision during their second year and subsequent summer, even before
being formally accepted as a student by a research advisor. Attend research seminars
and stay engaged with a potential advisor’s research group. Ask your proposed supervisor
if your course schedule and advanced coursework align with their current interests.
Be direct about your timeline: discuss funding, academic preparation, and your goals.
Work with them early to find out what’s needed before you can move on to the Oral
Exam. Different research groups have different expectations, but about a year of initial
research with your advisor (and perhaps advanced coursework) is a reasonable timeframe
for setting up the Oral Exam.
The Oral Exam and a commitment. The oral exam consists of a presentation of an approved research topic in physics
or astronomy to a committee of at least three faculty members, prepared under the
guidance of one of them. This exam is a demonstration that the student is capable
of beginning PhD-level research; it is not necessary to show a completed research
project. The oral exam may be a thesis proposal or an initial project together with
enough background material to provide context.
The faculty advisor for the oral exam will generally become the student’s thesis advisor.
Upon passing the exam, an advisor is asked to commit to supporting the student academically going forward, and, where possible, with funding.
The committee members must be approved in advance by the Graduate Program Director.
The committee should contain at least one experimentalist and one theorist, and at
least one member whose research specialty is different from the student’s field of
research. At least half of the committee, and the chair, must be full-time faculty,
and the chair cannot be the student’s future advisor.
Students are encouraged to complete the Oral Exam by the start of their sixth semester
at Stony Brook or earlier. The formal deadline is before the start of the seventh
semester (the start of their fourth year). Students may take the Oral Exam while still
completing their coursework and the Comprehensive Exam – there’s no requirement to
finish those first.
For how to assemble your committee, choose a topic, and submit the required forms,
see The Oral Exam in Resources.
The Doctoral Thesis and Defense
The Doctoral Thesis must present original research representing the student’s own
independent contribution. Although much research is collaborative, the thesis should
make clear which results are the student’s own, and the student must be able to defend
all of the work presented. Normally, the principal results have been published or
submitted for publication by the time of the defense. However, both the thesis and
the defense will be evaluated based on their substance rather than a specific publication
count.
The Doctoral Defense is an oral presentation of the written thesis before the Thesis
Defense Committee and is the last exam taken by a PhD student at Stony Brook. All
defense committees are subject to approval by the Graduate Program Director; usually,
the student’s Oral Exam committee serves as its core.
The committee has at least four members: at least three from the Department (full-time
or adjunct), typically the three members of the student’s Oral Exam Committee, plus
one external member from outside the Department – a scientist from another department
at Stony Brook or another institution, who is not a collaborator or co-author, and
who can give an independent evaluation of the thesis work. At least half of the committee,
including the chair, must be full-time faculty, and the chair cannot be the student’s
advisor. The committee should include at least one experimentalist, one theorist,
and one member from a research field other than the thesis topic; the external member
may also fill the experimentalist or theorist role.
The advisor, chair, and student must be physically present for the defense. Other
members are preferred to attend in person but may participate virtually.
For the full step-by-step checklist – filing for graduation, forming and getting your
committee approved, writing the thesis, submitting the defense announcement, and collecting
signatures and submitting to ProQuest – see the steps to The Doctoral Defense in Resources.
Graduate Funding
The sections below cover PhD tuition and funding – for current stipend and salary
figures, see Funding and Tuition on the Apply page.
Tuition
If properly handled, PhD students do not pay tuition, which is covered by a tuition
scholarship. However, serious problems can arise for those who fail to follow instructions,
respond to notices, or submit forms on time – sometimes resulting in large, irretrievable
financial losses. Two things put this coverage at risk if you don’t follow through
on them:
New York State residency. Establish residency as soon as you’re eligible – see New York State Residency in Resources for the requirements, documentation, and deadlines.
Your credit load. Register for the number of credits your tuition waiver requires each semester – see
Registering for Classes and Credits in Resources for the current requirements and what happens if you go over.
Support
Doctoral students are typically supported as a Teaching Assistant (TA) during their
first two years, as outlined in their offer letter. After that, students are expected
to find an advisor and move to research-grant support as a Research Assistant (RA).
Some students have different arrangements, for example through graduate fellowships.
Doctoral students can also be supported as a TA during the summer. The TA Allocation
Committee, described below, makes these decisions. First-year students requesting
summer support receive strong preference. In Fall 2026, for example, every first-year
student who requested summer support received eight weeks of it.
Additional Support. Students sometimes need additional funding. This can happen if a student has not
yet found an advisor able to provide funding, or if an advisor’s funding is unexpectedly
interrupted. In these cases, the Department may be able to provide extra TA support.
The TA Allocation Committee decides whether extra TA support should be provided. Its
members are the Graduate Program Director (Derek Teaney), the Graduate Coordinator
(Donald Sheehan), the Undergraduate Program Director (Dominik Schneble), and the Undergraduate
Astronomy Director (Michael Zingale). The committee weighs:
Availability of TA lines.
How many semesters of extra TA support the student has already received.
Whether the student is in good academic standing and making research progress.
The student’s past performance as a TA and their professional conduct.
Any mitigating factors.
A third-year student in good standing who needs more time to find an advisor or settle
into a research group will almost always receive additional funding. To date, the
only students denied this funding have had serious, ongoing problems with professional
conduct or with academic and research progress.
Professional Conduct
The sections below cover departmental and University policy on conduct, academic standing,
and leave – as distinct from the academic requirements and milestones described above.
Graduate students are expected to conduct themselves professionally – both in everyday
interactions with colleagues and in their research – and to meet the same ethical
standards as any other member of the University and physics communities.
Respect. Day-to-day conduct toward colleagues, students, and staff is governed by the University’s
Code of Student Responsibility, published by Community Standards, whose “Respect for Persons” provisions prohibit harassment and discrimination; sexual
misconduct is covered separately under Section VII. Concerns can be raised with the
Office of Equity and Access or Title IX. Because graduate students also teach, university policy additionally bars personal
or business relationships with students you supervise or grade.
Research. Research conduct falls under the University’s Responsible Conduct of Research and Scholarship policy; students on grant-funded research may be required to complete related training as
a condition of that funding. Fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism in research
are handled by the University’s Research Integrity Officer – see the Office of Research
Compliance’s Research Misconduct page for how to report a concern; the same behavior in coursework – including the
Comprehensive Exam – instead falls under the Academic Integrity Policy.
The APS Guidelines. For physicists specifically, the APS Ethics Standards are worth reading in full: they cover both halves of this at once – treating colleagues
and students fairly and respectfully, and conducting research honestly, including
proper authorship and prompt correction of honest error.
Violations of these standards, in fact or in spirit, are handled by the appropriate
University office: Community Standards for conduct, the Academic Judiciary for coursework integrity, the Office of Equity and Access for harassment and discrimination, Title IX for sexual misconduct, and the Office of Research Compliance’s Research Misconduct process for research. Decisions to dismiss or place a student on probation for conduct
are made by the Graduate School and these offices, not the Department. The Department’s
own Good Standing review below is reserved for academic progress, though professional conduct is also
a factor in ongoing TA support – see Support above.
Good Standing
Good standing means a student is meeting the requirements of the degree program and
making satisfactory progress toward the degree. A student can also lose good standing
through inappropriate conduct, as discussed in Professional Conduct above.
Responsibility for the Degree Requirements. A student is responsible for keeping their own degree steps on track and for contacting
the Graduate Program Director promptly when there are setbacks. Neglecting this responsibility
can also affect good standing, just like courses, the Comprehensive Exam, and progress
in research. Reach out early before missteps become a good-standing issue.
Advisor and Oral Exam. Students are expected to find an advisor and complete the Oral Exam by the formal deadline – before the start of their fourth year – since an advisor
is required both for the Oral Exam and for advancing to candidacy. The Oral Exam can
be repeated as long as the student is within this deadline. A student who reaches
the deadline without an advisor committed to continuing is no longer in good standing.
In this case, the student should speak to the Graduate Program Director and set up
a concrete schedule. If the issue is not resolved, the student will be placed on Departmental
Probation – see below.
Teaching. TA performance is evaluated each semester by the supervising faculty member. Sustained
unsatisfactory performance can put a student’s good standing at risk, and can result
in the loss of TA funding (see Teaching and Support above).
Core courses. Students are required to take the core courses, except if they passed the relevant
Comprehensive Exam at the Placement level or received a course waiver. If a student
doesn’t pass a core course with a grade of B or better, they can retake it, or petition
the Graduate Program Director to instead pass the Comprehensive Exam in that subject
at the PhD level – avoiding a retake this way is a discretionary decision by the Graduate
Program Director, not a formal make-up exam.
Comprehensive exam. If a PhD student has not passed the comprehensive exam at the beginning of their
fifth semester, the student should work with the Graduate Program Director to form
an ad hoc committee. This committee will be chaired by the Graduate Program Director
and will normally include the chair of the exam committee and any advisor if the student
has started working with a professor. Additional members as considered appropriate
may be added at the discretion of the Graduate Program Director. This committee will
decide whether the student will be given a replacement oral exam in the relevant subjects,
whether there are additional written comprehensive exam attempts to be given, or whether
they will have to leave the program. The criteria on which the decision will be made
include past performance on the comprehensive exam, the standing of the student with
regard to required courses, and their demonstrated potential to proceed to full-time
PhD research. It is the department’s general policy that if the progress on these
criteria is satisfactory a student will be granted an opportunity to either take the
written exam again or have a replacement oral exam. The format of the replacement
oral exam will be decided by the ad hoc committee and communicated to the student
prior to the exam, but often involves basic undergraduate questions to be answered
orally in an open dialogue with the committee. By working with the ad hoc committee,
the student should resolve the Comprehensive Exam requirements by the end of the third
academic year. A student who is asked to leave the program may appeal through the
Graduate School’s own Probation, Conduct and Grievances process.
Time limit to degree. Like all Stony Brook doctoral students, students must complete the PhD within seven
years of reaching 24 graduate-level credits (G4 status, usually the end of the first
year) – the Graduate School’s University-wide time limit. See Time Limit Extension in Resources for how to request more time if you need it – the request is reviewed
by the Graduate Program Director together with your advisor.
Letter of Concern. Before a situation rises to the level of formal probation, the Graduate Program Director
may send a student an informal Letter of Concern – flagging a specific problem (a
missed milestone, slow research progress, TA performance, etc.) and what’s expected
going forward. This is not a formal action and does not appear on a student’s record;
it’s meant to give a student the chance to correct course early.
Probation. The Graduate School applies its own academic standards to all doctoral programs:
a cumulative graduate GPA below 3.0 in courses numbered 500 or above triggers academic
probation, for a maximum of two semesters. A student must return their GPA to 3.0
by the end of the second probation semester or will not normally be permitted to continue
– see the Graduate Catalog’s Probation, Conduct and Grievances policy for the full requirements, including the required notification letter and
the process for appealing a decision.
Departmental Probation. In addition, the Department may place a student on probation for insufficient progress
on the degree requirements – for example, not finding an advisor or not passing the
Comprehensive Exam or Oral Exam on time. In this case, a probation committee will
be set up consisting of no fewer than three faculty, chaired by the Graduate Program
Director and including the student’s advisor, if one has been identified. Additional
members as considered appropriate may be added at the discretion of the Graduate Program
Director. This committee will evaluate the student’s overall progress in the degree
program and set a realistic timeframe – usually one semester – to address the identified
issues. A student who remains on probation past this timeframe, without resolving
or progressing on the underlying issues, may be dismissed from the program, at the
discretion of the probation committee.
Appeal. A student who believes they have been unfairly dismissed may appeal. The primary
avenue is the Program Grievance and Appeals Committee (GPGAC), described in the Graduate
School’s Probation, Conduct and Grievances policy – an ad hoc committee, with no fewer than four members split evenly between
faculty and graduate students, that the student must request be convened. The GPGAC’s
review is limited to whether proper procedure was followed and policy was fairly applied
– it does not re-evaluate the underlying academic judgment, such as whether the student
had in fact met the degree requirements. If the matter isn’t resolved at this level,
it can be escalated to the Dean of the Graduate School and, from there, the Graduate
Council Appeals Committee (GCAC), whose decision is advisory to the Dean; the decision
of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education is final.
Leave of Absence
Parental Leave. Eligible students can take up to 12 weeks of leave for a birth, or 6 weeks for an
adoption or foster placement. You’ll keep your full-time registered status, benefits,
and funding, plus get an automatic one-semester extension on program deadlines. See
the Graduate School’s Parental Leave Policy for eligibility, and submit the Parental Leave Application with supporting documentation, ideally 30 days ahead. International students should
also check with Visa and Immigration Services.
Other Leave (e.g., Medical Leave). If you need to take leave for another reason, such as a medical issue, we want to
make this as manageable as possible. Submit a Request for Leave of Absence form to the Graduate School. The Graduate Catalog covers the full policy and is worth reading. A leave is typically granted for up
to a year, and can be extended for an additional year on review.
If possible, work out a re-entry plan with the Graduate Program Director and your
advisor. You can use the Re-Entry Plan Template on the Graduate School’s Student Resources page as a starting point. The plan should cover funding, and whether your research
will remain timely when you return. In the current funding environment, we can’t promise
your grant funding will still be available upon your return, but if it isn’t, the
TA Allocation Committee described above can consider funding you as a TA.
Astronomy & Biology Concentrations
Beyond the standard PhD, we offer two concentrations for students with more specific
interests. Each has slightly different requirements from the default track, particularly
around the breadth and laboratory courses.
Astronomy Concentration
Students may elect to earn a PhD in Physics with a concentration in Astronomy. (Note: you can work with an advisor in Astronomy without earning this concentration.) To
complete the PhD with this concentration, students need to take three courses chosen
from PHY 521, 522, 523, 524 (the core astronomy sequence) and PHY 620 (Modern General
Relativity) – that is, any three out of the five. The four core astronomy courses
rotate on a four-semester cycle, one course per semester, while PHY 620 is offered
every year. Students completing the astronomy concentration satisfy the standard breadth requirement in this manner. A possible astronomy sequence looks like this:

Physical Biology Concentration
This is an interdisciplinary concentration in connection with the Laufer Center for
quantitative biology. Students usually declare their interest in this concentration
not later than the end of the first semester. Postponing this decision will result
in a loss of time. The main difference with the default physics concentration is a
reduction of core courses by one course while several physical biology courses are
required. Instead of the graduate lab students do rotations with faculty associated
with the Laufer center. Also the Graduate Seminar is substituted by the Laufer Center
Journal Club. The requirements for a PhD Degree in Physics with Concentration in Physical
Biology are as follows:
Four Physics core courses: Electrodynamics (PHY 505), Quantum Mechanics I (PHY 511),
Statistical Mechanics (PHY 540) and either Classical Mechanics (PHY 501) or Quantum Mechanics II (PHY 512).
Two Core Courses in Physical Biology: Physical Biology (PHY 558) and Biological Dynamics
and Networks (PHY 559)
Biology For Physical Scientists (PHY 561)
Two semesters of Teaching (PHY 600)
Two semesters of Lab Rotations (PHY 584 / AMS 531)
Two semesters of the Laufer Center Journal Club (PHY 665 / AMS 532)
Two Life Science courses from an approved list. Currently, the following courses have
been approved: Biomolecular Structure and Analysis (CHE 541), Molecular Genetics (MCB
503), Structural Biology and Spectroscopy (MCB 512), Graduate Biochemistry I (MCB
520), Cell Biology (MCB 656), Introduction to Neuroscience I (BNB 561), and Introduction
to Neuroscience II (BNB 562)
Passing of the Comprehensive Exam.
An oral exam on a topic in Physical Biology
Student should find an advisor working on the topic of Physical Biology
All courses have to be passed with a grade of B or better.
